text: Every table needs a primary key, and most of the time you want the database to generate it for you. Let's compare how identity, sequence, auto_increment, and serial each solve the exact same problem.
SQL Server's approach is identity, with a seed and an increment, as a column property. The database tracks and generates the next value automatically every time you insert a row.

Oracle's traditional approach is more hands-on: create a sequence object, then a before-insert trigger that pulls the next sequence value into the column. This is the classic pattern you'll see in a lot of existing Oracle schemas.

Modern Oracle, twelve c and later, also supports a generated always as identity syntax that looks much more like SQL Server. Under the hood, it's still a sequence -- the trigger boilerplate is just handled for you now.

MySQL is the most direct of the four: auto_increment is just a column attribute, no separate object required. PostgreSQL's serial, meanwhile, is really shorthand that creates a sequence for you behind the scenes -- or you can use the modern generated always as identity syntax instead.
